questions.text: Which of the following best describes a 'Special Mention Account (SMA)' in the context of early NPA identification?

options.text: An account where borrower has requested loan restructuring
An account showing signs of stress before it becomes NPA
An account flagged for fraud investigation
An account written off partially by the bank
An account of wilful defaulters only

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is An account showing signs of stress before it becomes NPA.

Key Points

  • Special Mention Accounts (SMA) were introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to identify incipient stress in the assets of banks and financial institutions at an early stage.
  • An account is classified as SMA when the principal or interest payment is overdue or the account shows symptoms of bad health, even if it has not yet completed the 90-day period required to be classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). Hence, statement B is correct.
  • The SMA classification is divided into three sub-categories based on the duration of the delay in payment: SMA-0, SMA-1, and SMA-2.
  • SMA-0: This represents accounts where the principal or interest payment is not overdue for more than 30 days, but the account shows signs of incipient stress.
  • SMA-1: This includes accounts where the overdue period is between 31 to 60 days.
  • SMA-2: This category covers accounts where the overdue period is between 61 to 90 days.
  • Loan restructuring is a remedial measure taken after identifying stress or default, rather than the definition of the account category itself. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • SMA is a classification for credit risk and liquidity stress, whereas fraud investigation involves different regulatory protocols like Red Flagged Accounts (RFA). Hence, statement C is incorrect.
  • An account that is written off is removed from the balance sheet as an unrecoverable loss, which occurs long after the SMA and NPA stages. Hence, statement D is incorrect.
  • A wilful defaulter is a specific legal designation for a borrower who has the ability to pay but deliberately avoids repayment; SMA applies to all accounts showing stress regardless of the borrower's intent. Hence, statement E is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • The RBI introduced the SMA framework in 2014 as part of the "Framework for Revitalizing Distressed Assets in the Economy."
  • The Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC) was established to collect, store, and disseminate data on all systemic exposures of Rs. 5 crore and above.
  • Banks are required to report credit information to CRILC on a monthly basis, including the SMA status of large borrowers, to ensure transparency and early collective action.
  • The 90-day norm for NPAs means that if an account remains in the SMA-2 stage and exceeds 90 days of overdue, it must be downgraded to a Sub-standard asset.
  • The primary objective of SMA categorization is to trigger a Corrective Action Plan (CAP), which may include rectification, restructuring, or recovery proceedings.

Important Points

  • Incipient Stress Indicators: Apart from payment delays, SMA-0 can be triggered by non-financial signals such as a drop in credit rating, frequent cheque bounces, or a significant delay in project completion.
  • Asset Classification: Once an account stays as an NPA for a period up to 12 months, it is called a Sub-standard asset. If it remains NPA for more than 12 months, it becomes a Doubtful asset.
  • Provisioning: Banks must set aside capital (provisions) based on the classification. While SMA accounts do not always require higher provisioning like NPAs, they serve as a buffer for banks to manage liquidity risk.
  • Regulatory Updates: In 2021, the RBI clarified that the out-of-order status for Cash Credit/Overdraft (CC/OD) accounts is also a critical metric for SMA and NPA identification to prevent evergreening of loans.

questions.text: Under IBC 2016, which authority oversees the insolvency resolution process for corporate debtors?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).

Key Points

  • The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) is the designated Adjudicating Authority for the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) and liquidation of corporate debtors under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. Hence, the statement regarding NCLT is correct.
  • The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was enacted to provide a time-bound process for resolving insolvency in India, aiming to maximize the value of assets and promote entrepreneurship.
  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) acts as the central banking institution and regulator of the banking system but does not oversee the insolvency resolution process itself; however, it can initiate the process for Financial Service Providers under specific rules. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
  • The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is the regulatory body for the securities market in India and does not function as an adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
  • The Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) serves as the adjudicating authority for insolvency resolution and bankruptcy of individuals and partnership firms, rather than corporate bodies, under the IBC 2016. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
  • The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial body and acts as the final appellate authority for cases arising from the NCLAT, but it does not oversee the primary resolution process of corporate debtors. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Establishment of NCLT: The National Company Law Tribunal was constituted on 1 June 2016 under Section 408 of the Companies Act, 2013. It has several benches across India, with the Principal Bench located in New Delhi.
  • The IBC Ecosystem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), established on 1 October 2016, is the regulatory body that oversees Insolvency Professionals (IP), Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPA), and Information Utilities (IU).
  • Appellate Authority: Any person aggrieved by an order of the NCLT may file an appeal with the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT). Appeals against NCLAT orders are further heard by the Supreme Court of India on a point of law.
  • Resolution Timelines: Initially, the IBC mandated a 180-day period for the CIRP, extendable by 90 days. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2019, later specified that the process must be completed within a mandatory total period of 330 days, including any extension and time taken in legal proceedings.
  • Moratorium: Upon the admission of an application by the NCLT, a moratorium is declared under Section 14, which prohibits the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits against the corporate debtor to ensure a smooth resolution.

Important Points

  • Corporate Debtor: Refers to a corporate person who owes a debt to any person. The IBC applies to companies incorporated under the Companies Act or any previous company law, and Limited Liability Partnerships (LLP).
  • Committee of Creditors (CoC): Once the IRP is appointed, they constitute a CoC consisting of all financial creditors. The CoC holds the power to approve or reject a Resolution Plan with a minimum 66% voting share.
  • Insolvency Professionals (IPs): These are licensed professionals who take over the management of the corporate debtor during the CIRP, ensuring the company remains a going concern while a resolution is sought.
  • Information Utilities (IU): These are centralized repositories of financial information that validate and store data regarding loans and defaults, helping the NCLT quickly ascertain the occurrence of a default.
  • Financial vs. Operational Creditors: Financial Creditors (like banks) are those whose relationship is a pure financial contract, while Operational Creditors (like suppliers) are those whose liabilities arise from the provision of goods or services.

questions.text: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted in which year for time-bound resolution of stressed assets and NPAs?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 2016.

Key Points

  • The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted by the Parliament of India in May 2016 to consolidate the existing framework by creating a single law for insolvency and bankruptcy. Hence, the year 2016 is correct.
  • The bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2015 and was subsequently passed by the Lok Sabha on 5th May 2016 and by the Rajya Sabha on 11th May 2016.
  • The IBC 2016 received the Presidential assent on 28th May 2016, marking a significant reform in the Indian economic legal landscape to handle Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) and stressed assets.
  • The code was formulated based on the recommendations of the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC), which was headed by Dr. T. K. Viswanathan.
  • It aims to promote entrepreneurship and the availability of credit by ensuring the time-bound resolution of insolvency cases, which was previously delayed under multiple laws like SICA 1985 and SARFAESI 2002.

Additional Information

  • Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI):
    • Established on 1st October 2016, the IBBI serves as the regulatory body for overseeing insolvency proceedings and entities like Insolvency Professionals (IPs) and Information Utilities (IUs).
    • It has regulatory oversight over the Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs) and is responsible for the implementation of the IBC.
  • Adjudicating Authorities:
    • The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) acts as the adjudicating authority for corporate persons and Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs).
    • The Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) is the adjudicating authority for individuals and unlimited partnership firms.
  • Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP):
    • Under Section 4 of the code, CIRP can be initiated if the default amount is at least Rs. 1 crore (increased from Rs. 1 lakh in 2020 to protect MSMEs).
    • The process must be completed within a mandatory period of 330 days, which includes any time taken in legal proceedings.
  • The Committee of Creditors (CoC):
    • The CoC, primarily comprising financial creditors, is the supreme decision-making body in the resolution process.
    • A resolution plan requires the approval of 66% of the voting share of the CoC to be implemented.

Important Points

  • Section 29A: This was an amendment introduced in November 2017 to disqualify wilful defaulters and certain other persons from submitting a resolution plan, ensuring that defaulting promoters do not regain control of the company at a discount.
  • Pre-packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP): Introduced in April 2021, this provides an efficient alternative resolution mechanism for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), allowing for a quicker, consensual restructuring.
  • Waterfall Mechanism: Under Section 53, the code specifies the priority of distribution of assets during liquidation, where secured creditors and workmen's dues for 24 months are given top priority after the costs of the insolvency process.
  • Global Context: The IBC 2016 significantly improved India's ranking in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business Index, particularly in the "Resolving Insolvency" parameter, moving from 136th to 52nd position within a few years of implementation.

questions.text: Under RBI guidelines, which of the following is a tool used by banks to resolve NPAs by converting debt into equity shares of the borrower company?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR).

Key Points

  • Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in June 2015 to provide banks with more power to recover loans from stressed companies.
  • Under this scheme, the Joint Lenders' Forum (JLF) or the consortium of banks was authorized to convert a portion of the borrower company’s debt into equity shares. Hence, the statement regarding debt-to-equity conversion is correct.
  • The primary function of SDR was to allow banks to take over management control of a defaulting company by holding at least 51% of the equity shares. This was intended to facilitate the sale of the company to a new promoter.
  • One-Time Settlement (OTS) involves a compromise where the bank agrees to accept a payment less than the total dues to settle the loan account. This does not involve converting debt into equity. Hence, this option is not the primary tool for conversion.
  • SARFAESI enforcement refers to the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, which allows banks to seize and sell collateral assets without court intervention. Hence, this is an enforcement tool rather than a restructuring conversion tool.

Additional Information

  • Non-Performing Assets (NPAs):
    • An NPA is a loan or advance for which the principal or interest payment remained overdue for a period of 90 days.
    • Classification: NPAs are categorized into Sub-standard assets (less than or equal to 12 months), Doubtful assets (exceeding 12 months), and Loss assets (identified as uncollectible by the bank or RBI).
  • The SARFAESI Act, 2002:
    • Enacted in 2002, this Act empowers banks and financial institutions to recover their Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) by seizing the security provided by the borrower.
    • It is applicable only to secured loans where the loan amount is more than Rs. 1 Lakh and the remaining debt is more than 20% of the principal and interest.
  • Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016:
    • The IBC was introduced in 2016 to provide a time-bound process (usually 180 to 270 days) for insolvency resolution.
    • It replaced several older mechanisms including SDR and CDR to streamline the recovery process through the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
  • Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR):
    • A mechanism established in 2001 for the reorganization of liabilities of companies facing financial stress.
    • It aimed to provide liquidity and viability to the debtor by adjusting the repayment schedule or reducing the interest rate.

Important Points

  • Feb 12, 2018 Circular: The RBI issued a landmark circular on February 12, 2018, which abolished all existing restructuring schemes like SDR, S4A (Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets), and CDR.
  • Lok Adalats: These are alternative dispute resolution forums. For banks, they are generally used for the settlement of NPAs where the loan amount does not exceed Rs. 20 Lakhs.
  • Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs): These are specialized financial institutions that buy the NPAs from banks at a discounted rate and attempt to recover the dues directly from the borrowers.
  • The SDR framework required banks to find a new buyer for the equity within 18 months of the reference date to avoid asset classification downgrades.

options.text: Gross NPA − Provisions held against NPAs

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Gross NPA − Provisions held against NPAs.

Key Points

  • Net NPA (Non-Performing Asset) is a financial metric used by banks to reflect the actual value of their bad loans after accounting for the safety cushions or provisions set aside.
  • Gross NPA represents the total value of all loan assets that have been classified as non-performing according to the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) guidelines, typically when interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days.
  • Provisions are the funds that banks must set aside from their profits to cover potential losses arising from bad loans. This act of setting aside capital is known as provisioning.
  • The calculation Gross NPA − Provisions provides a more realistic picture of the bank's financial health, as it shows the net loss exposure that is not yet covered by capital buffers. Hence, the statement regarding Option B is correct.
  • The Net NPA Ratio is often calculated as (Net NPAs ÷ Net Advances) × 100, which helps investors and regulators understand the asset quality of the banking institution.

Additional Information

  • Asset Classification: Banks in India categorize assets into four groups: Standard Assets (regular payments), Sub-standard Assets (NPA for ≤ 12 months), Doubtful Assets (NPA for > 12 months), and Loss Assets (identified as uncollectible by the bank or RBI).
  • Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR): This is the ratio of provisioning to Gross NPAs. A higher PCR (typically above 70%) indicates that the bank is well-buffered against potential defaults and has a lower Net NPA.
  • SARFAESI Act, 2002: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act allows banks to auction residential or commercial properties of borrowers to recover NPAs without the intervention of a court.
  • Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016: This legislation was introduced to provide a time-bound process for insolvency resolution of corporate debtors, significantly aiding in the reduction of Gross NPAs in the Indian banking sector.
  • Impact on Profitability: High NPAs lead to increased provisioning requirements, which directly reduces the Net Profit of the bank and limits its capacity to lend further, creating a liquidity crunch in the economy.

Important Points

  • Provisioning Norms: For Sub-standard assets, a general provision of 15% is required. For Doubtful assets, the provisioning varies from 25% to 100% depending on the period for which the asset has remained doubtful and the availability of security/collateral.
  • Written-off Accounts: These are loans that the bank no longer expects to recover and removes from its balance sheet. While they reduce the Gross NPA figure, the bank continues its recovery efforts against the borrower.
  • Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR): High Net NPAs can erode a bank's capital, making it difficult to maintain the CAR mandated by Basel III norms, which currently stands at a minimum of 9% for Indian banks.
  • Twin Balance Sheet Problem: A term coined in the Economic Survey of India, referring to the stressed balance sheets of both Public Sector Banks (PSBs) due to NPAs and corporate sectors due to over-leveraged debt.

questions.text: What is the full form of PCR in the context of NPA management?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Provisioning Coverage Ratio.

Key Points

  • Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) is a vital financial metric used in the banking sector to measure the extent to which a bank has set aside funds to cover potential losses from Non-Performing Assets (NPAs).
  • It is calculated as the ratio of the total provisions held by a bank (excluding technical write-offs) to its Gross NPAs, expressed as a percentage.
  • A higher PCR indicates that the bank has a larger buffer to manage the credit risk associated with bad loans, making it more resilient to asset quality shocks. Hence, option B is the correct definition.
  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) historically suggested a benchmark PCR of 70% for banks to ensure financial stability and transparency in their balance sheets.
  • This ratio helps investors and regulators assess the health of a bank’s loan portfolio and its ability to absorb loan losses without impacting its core capital.

Additional Information

  • Non-Performing Assets (NPA):
    • An asset becomes an NPA when the principal or interest payment remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days in the case of a term loan.
    • NPAs are further classified into three categories: Sub-standard assets (overdue for ≤ 12 months), Doubtful assets (overdue for > 12 months), and Loss assets (identified as uncollectible by the bank or RBI).
  • Gross NPA vs. Net NPA:
    • Gross NPA is the total value of all loan defaults by the bank's customers across all branches.
    • Net NPA is calculated by subtracting the provisions (the PCR amount) from the Gross NPA. It represents the actual burden of bad loans on the bank’s books.
  • Provisioning Norms:
    • The RBI mandates banks to follow specific provisioning norms based on the age of the NPA. For instance, a 15% provision is usually required for Sub-standard (unsecured) assets, while 100% is required for Loss assets.
    • The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 has also played a significant role in the recovery process of these NPAs in India.

Important Points

  • Financial Stability Report (FSR): The RBI publishes the FSR twice a year, which provides data on the PCR levels of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) to monitor the systemic risk in the Indian economy.
  • Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR): While PCR focuses on covering specific loan losses, the CAR (or CRAR) ensures that the bank has enough equity capital to protect depositors. Both are critical for a bank's survival during an economic slowdown.
  • Evolution of PCR: In recent years (specifically post-2018), many Indian banks have significantly increased their PCR, often exceeding 75-80%, to clean up their balance sheets following the Asset Quality Review (AQR).
  • Impact on Profitability: Higher provisioning (resulting in a higher PCR) reduces a bank’s Net Profit in the short term, as more income is diverted to create the reserve, but it strengthens the long-term sustainability of the organization.

questions.text: A loan account where the borrower has paid all overdue amounts and the account has been regular for a specified period is called?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Upgraded Asset.

Key Points

  • An Upgraded Asset is a loan account that was previously classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) but has been reclassified as a Standard Asset. This happens when the borrower pays all the overdue interest and principal amounts, making the account regular. Hence, statement C is correct.
  • According to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines, an NPA can be upgraded to a standard asset only if the entire arrears of interest and principal are paid by the borrower.
  • The process of upgradation ensures that the bank’s balance sheet reflects the improved creditworthiness of the borrower. It allows the financial institution to reduce its provisioning requirements, thereby increasing its net profit.
  • Once a loan is upgraded, it is no longer subject to the strict monitoring and legal recovery processes associated with distressed assets, provided the borrower continues to meet future repayment schedules.
  • A Restructured Asset is an account where the bank grants concessions to a borrower facing financial difficulties, such as extending the repayment period or reducing interest rates. It does not necessarily mean the account has been regularized by full payment of dues. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • A Written-off Asset is a loan that the bank considers uncollectible and removes from its active books to clean up the balance sheet, although recovery efforts may still continue through legal channels. Hence, statement B is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Non-Performing Asset (NPA): In India, an asset becomes non-performing when it ceases to generate income for the bank. For most loans, this period is defined as 90 days of overdue status for interest or principal.
  • Asset Classification: Banks are required to classify NPAs into three categories: Sub-standard (overdue for less than or equal to 12 months), Doubtful (overdue for more than 12 months), and Loss Assets (where loss is identified but not written off).
  • Special Mention Accounts (SMA): Before an account turns into an NPA, it is classified as SMA to alert the bank. SMA-0 covers 1-30 days, SMA-1 covers 31-60 days, and SMA-2 covers 61-90 days of overdue.
  • SARFAESI Act, 2002: This Act allows banks and financial institutions to auction residential or commercial properties to recover loans when the borrower defaults on repayments.
  • Provisioning: Banks must set aside a specific percentage of funds from their profits as a buffer against bad loans. For a Standard Asset, the provision is typically 0.40%, whereas for Sub-standard assets, it can be 15%.

Important Points

  • Specified Period: For restructured accounts, the account must demonstrate satisfactory performance during a specified period (usually one year) before it can be upgraded to standard.
  • Income Recognition: According to RBI norms, banks can only recognize income from NPAs on a cash basis (when actually received), but for Standard or Upgraded Assets, income can be recognized on an accrual basis.
  • Watch-list Assets: These are Standard Assets where the bank perceives a high risk of slippage into the NPA category due to industry-specific or borrower-specific issues. Hence, statement E is incorrect.
  • Rescheduled Asset: This involves modifying the repayment schedule of a loan, often by granting a moratorium, without necessarily regularizing the arrears immediately. Hence, statement D is incorrect.

questions.text: Which of the following accounts will NOT be classified as NPA even if overdue for more than 90 days?

options.text: Agricultural loan account during natural calamity with RBI relaxation

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Agricultural loan account during natural calamity with RBI relaxation.

Key Points

  • According to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines, a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) is a loan or an advance where the interest and/or installment of principal remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days in respect of a Term Loan. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • In the case of Cash Credit (CC) or Overdraft (OD), an account is classified as NPA if it remains out of order for a period of more than 90 days. Hence, statement B is incorrect.
  • For Agricultural Loans, the NPA classification is linked to crop seasons instead of the 90-day rule. A loan granted for short duration crops is treated as NPA if the installment remains overdue for two crop seasons, while for long duration crops, the period is one crop season.
  • When a natural calamity (such as floods, drought, etc.) occurs, the RBI issues specific Master Circulars allowing banks to restructure or reschedule loans. In such cases, the account is not classified as NPA even if the overdue exceeds 90 days, provided the restructuring is done as per RBI relaxations. Hence, statement C is correct.
  • Housing loans and Personal loans are generally categorized under retail loans and strictly follow the 90-day overdue norm for NPA classification unless specific moratoriums are announced by the Government of India or RBI. Hence, statements D and E are incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Asset Classification Categories:
    • Standard Assets: These are accounts which do not disclose any problems and which do not carry more than normal risk attached to the business.
    • Sub-standard Assets: An asset which has remained NPA for a period less than or equal to 12 months.
    • Doubtful Assets: An asset would be classified as doubtful if it has remained in the sub-standard category for a period of 12 months.
    • Loss Assets: These are assets where loss has been identified by the bank, internal/external auditors, or the RBI inspection but the amount has not been written off wholly.
  • Special Mention Accounts (SMA):
    • Before a loan account turns into an NPA, it is classified as SMA to alert the bank about potential default.
    • SMA-0: Principal or interest payment not overdue for more than 30 days but showing signs of incipient stress.
    • SMA-1: Overdue between 31 to 60 days.
    • SMA-2: Overdue between 61 to 90 days.

Important Points

  • Relief Measures for Natural Calamities: Under the RBI Master Direction on Relief Measures by Banks in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities, banks are permitted to convert Short-Term Production Loans into Medium-Term Loans.
  • Moratorium Period: In areas affected by natural calamities, banks may grant a moratorium period of at least one year, and the rescheduled installment will not be treated as overdue for the purpose of NPA classification.
  • Income Recognition: For any NPA account, interest income is recognized by banks only when it is actually realized (Cash Basis), whereas for Standard Assets, it is recognized on an accrual basis.
  • Provisioning Norms: Banks are required to set aside a certain percentage of their profits as provisions for NPAs. For Sub-standard assets, a general provision of 15% is required, while for Doubtful assets, it ranges from 25% to 100% depending on the period for which the asset has remained doubtful.

questions.text: Which committee's recommendations formed the basis for NPA norms and prudential regulations introduced in India in the early 1990s?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Narasimham Committee. Key Points
  • The Narasimham Committee I (Committee on the Financial System) was appointed by the Government of India in August 1991 under the chairmanship of M. Narasimham, the 13th Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Hence, this committee is the correct basis for NPA norms.
  • The committee’s recommendations aimed at enhancing the transparency and efficiency of the banking sector, leading to the introduction of Prudential Norms for Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning.
  • It proposed the categorization of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) into four groups: Standard Assets, Sub-standard Assets, Doubtful Assets, and Loss Assets, based on the duration for which the principal or interest remained overdue.
  • A major recommendation was the reduction of the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) from 38.5% to 25% and the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to facilitate better liquidity flow into the productive sectors of the economy.
  • The committee also advocated for the adoption of the Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) in alignment with the Basel I standards, initially setting a target of 8% to strengthen the capital base of Indian banks.
Additional Information
  • Rangarajan Committee: This committee, headed by C. Rangarajan, is primarily known for its reports on Disinvestment of Shares in Public Sector Enterprises (1993) and the Methodology for Measurement of Poverty (2012). It did not formulate the initial 1990s NPA norms. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • Kelkar Committee: Led by Vijay Kelkar, this committee is renowned for its recommendations on Tax Reforms (Direct and Indirect taxes) in 2002 and Revisiting and Revitalizing the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model in 2015. Hence, statement C is incorrect.
  • Raghuram Rajan Committee: Formed in 2007 and submitting its report in 2008, the Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (CFSR) proposed "A Hundred Small Steps" to improve financial inclusion and promote a market-led financial system. Hence, statement D is incorrect.
  • Deepak Mohanty Committee: This committee was constituted by the RBI in 2015 to work on the Medium-term Path on Financial Inclusion. It also worked on the Base Rate system and monetary policy transmission. Hence, statement E is incorrect.
Important Points
  • The Narasimham Committee II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms) was established in 1998 to review the progress of the 1991 reforms and suggested the creation of Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) to handle bad debts.
  • Under current RBI guidelines, a loan or advance is classified as an NPA if the interest or installment remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days.
  • The implementation of these norms in the early 1990s marked the transition of the Indian banking system from social banking to commercial banking based on profitability and sustainability.
  • These reforms were part of the broader Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) strategy initiated by the then Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh during the Narasimha Rao government.

questions.text: As per RBI's IRAC norms, the full form of IRAC is?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Income Recognition and Asset Classification.

Key Points

  • IRAC stands for Income Recognition and Asset Classification. These norms are the prudential guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to ensure that the financial statements of banks reflect their actual financial health.
  • The primary objective of IRAC norms is to provide a uniform and consistent framework for Indian banks to recognize income and classify their assets (loans and advances) based on the associated credit risk. Hence, the correct option is Income Recognition and Asset Classification.
  • Under Income Recognition, banks are prohibited from recognizing income on Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) on an accrual basis. Instead, such income should be recognized only when it is actually realized or received.
  • Asset Classification refers to the process where banks categorize their credit facilities into Standard Assets and Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). This classification is further divided into Sub-standard, Doubtful, and Loss assets based on the period for which the asset has remained non-performing.
  • The RBI issues these guidelines through a Master Circular titled "Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances," which is updated periodically to maintain the stability of the banking sector.

Additional Information

  • Non-Performing Asset (NPA): An asset, including a leased asset, becomes non-performing when it ceases to generate income for the bank. For term loans, it is classified as an NPA if the interest or installment of principal remains overdue for more than 90 days.
  • Classification Categories:
    • Standard Assets: These are performing assets that do not disclose any problems and do not carry more than normal risk.
    • Sub-standard Assets: An asset that has remained an NPA for a period less than or equal to 12 months.
    • Doubtful Assets: An asset that has remained in the sub-standard category for a period exceeding 12 months.
    • Loss Assets: Assets where loss has been identified by the bank, internal/external auditors, or the RBI inspectors, but the amount has not been written off yet.
  • Provisioning Norms: Based on the IRAC classification, banks are required to make provisions. For Standard Assets, the provision usually ranges from 0.25% to 1.00% depending on the sector. For Sub-standard assets, a general provision of 15% of the outstanding amount is required.
  • Out of Order: For Cash Credit (CC) or Overdraft (OD) accounts, the account is treated as "out of order" if the outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit for 90 days.

Important Points

  • Special Mention Accounts (SMA): Before a loan becomes an NPA, it is categorized under SMA to identify incipient stress.
    • SMA-0: Principal or interest payment not overdue for more than 30 days but showing signs of incipient stress.
    • SMA-1: Overdue between 31 to 60 days.
    • SMA-2: Overdue between 61 to 90 days.
  • Agricultural Advances: The 90-day norm does not apply here. Instead, a loan is an NPA if the installment remains overdue for two crop seasons for short-duration crops or one crop season for long-duration crops.
  • Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR): This is the ratio of provisioning to gross NPAs, indicating the cushion a bank has to absorb losses. The RBI often monitors this to ensure financial stability.
  • Income Reversal: If an account becomes an NPA, any interest calculated and credited to the income account in the previous periods but not realized must be reversed or provided for in the current period.
